The Carnitas I Couldn’t Eat

My first week on a GLP-1 medicine, I made carnitas. Pork shoulder, orange, a stick of cinnamon, four hours in a low oven until the edges went dark and crackled. Teo had two helpings and said something kind about the orange.

I managed three bites and set my fork down.

Not wouldn’t. Couldn’t. A forkful of pork shoulder had turned into homework.

An empty plate can tell you what you managed at one sitting. It cannot tell you what your body needs across a day, or why a symptom is happening. Anita, my nurse practitioner, is thorough. Still, there is a gap between a good appointment and standing in your kitchen at six in the evening, looking at the pan you cooked and wondering what to do next.

That gap is what this book is for.

What went quiet, and what didn’t

The short version of the biology, which Chapter 10 explains in more detail: the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases describes semaglutide as mimicking GLP-1 signaling that affects brain areas involved in appetite and food intake. Tirzepatide mimics both GIP and GLP-1 signaling. These medicines can reduce appetite, but a quieter appetite does not tell you what amount or pattern of food and fluid is right for you.

Eating too little overall and losing weight can put muscle at risk. Chapter 11 will help you agree on an appropriate protein target with your dietitian or prescriber. Strength, food and fluid needs can depend on your health and other medicines; a general book cannot set those needs for you.

The NIDDK’s prescription-medications page says these medicines work best alongside a program of healthy eating and physical activity; they do not replace either. True, and hard to put into practice when half a sandwich feels like plenty. This book stays with that practical gap: what to ask, what to notice, and how to work with your own care team instead of borrowing a stranger’s plan.

If a condition, another medicine, or a clinician’s instruction changes what is safe for you, take that detail to your prescriber or pharmacist. The point is not to force yourself into a standard routine. It is to find a workable one with the people who know your care.

Two rules I cook by

Two habits shape the book. They are starting points, not substitutes for advice about your own health.

The first: make a plan for eating that does not depend entirely on appetite. Chapter 11 covers protein with a dietitian or prescriber, then breaks the day into manageable choices. Fluid needs are personal too; ask your clinician how to plan fluids if you have limits or side effects.

The second: every question with a dose in it belongs with your prescriber. Not a forum, not a relative taking the same medicine, and not this book. Whether to start, raise, lower, skip, pause or stop is a decision to make with your prescriber, who can consider your situation. When a chapter brushes up against that line, it will point you toward the right conversation rather than guess at an answer. Chapter 20 is for planning any medication change with your prescriber.

These two habits are a starting point, not a substitute for your medicine’s safety information; read the Chapter 10 warning card and your current label before relying on this book.

Three things this book is not

This book is general information, not legal, financial, or medical advice. Its narrator uses a pen name, and personal stories are composites written to illustrate real situations. Rules and product instructions change; confirm health decisions with the professionals who know your care.

Keep your exact product guide nearby. Use this book to prepare questions, not to change treatment. Start with Chapter 10’s warning card, then go to the chapter that matches today’s problem.

It’s not a cookbook. There are recipes here and there, usually because a technique needs a demonstration, but if you came for ninety days of dinners you’ll be disappointed and you should get your money back. The problem most of us have is not a shortage of recipes. It’s a plate we can’t finish.

It’s not a dosing guide. No milligrams, no titration schedules, no opinions about what week you should be on what. I have read enough internet threads where strangers trade dose advice to know how confidently wrong people can be about someone else’s prescription.

And it’s not medical advice. Dana Whitfield is a pen-name narrator, and my first-person scenes, like the other stories here, are composites. They illustrate a problem; they do not prove that a real author used these medicines or that a habit is safe. The named people are composites too. The facts and safety information come from the agencies and current product labels named in the text; when a decision depends on your health or prescription, take it to your care team.

The help here is kitchen-level: ways to discuss protein with a dietitian, questions to bring to an appointment, and small routines to consider with your clinician. It is not evidence that a particular habit is safe for every reader.

When to shut the book and call someone

If you become dizzy or faint, do not assume a missed protein meal explains it. Follow your diabetes team’s low-glucose plan if you have one; contact a clinician promptly. If a symptom is new, worsening, severe, or you are unsure how urgent it is, stop reading. For trouble breathing, swelling of the face, throat, or tongue, fainting, severe confusion, or another immediately dangerous symptom, seek emergency help now. Otherwise, use the emergency instructions in your current Medication Guide and contact your prescriber or pharmacist.

How it’s laid out

Chapter 11 turns the protein question into small choices across an ordinary day; Chapter 12 covers strength work and a readiness check.

Read in whatever order helps; no suggested order should delay medical attention. Later chapters are available when you want help preparing for a prescriber conversation, keeping a simple record, navigating social meals or insurance questions, and building routines around the life you actually have. You do not need to make every change at once, and a checklist is a prompt for a conversation, not a test you can pass or fail. Each substantive chapter has one you can adapt with your care team; skip anything that conflicts with their instructions.

Chapter 10: What Is Actually Happening

The pharmacy bag sits beside your mug. On your phone, one page calls the medicine by its brand name; another mentions a drug with the same active ingredient and a different name. At dinner, you put down your fork sooner than expected. The label is full of cautions, the internet is full of confident explanations, and your body has given you one plain fact: this feels different.

A signal, not a character test

Semaglutide and tirzepatide act on hormone pathways involved in appetite. On its prescription-medications page, NIDDK explains that semaglutide copies a gut-hormone signal called GLP-1, which is associated with appetite and food intake. Tirzepatide engages GIP and GLP-1 receptors, also affecting appetite-related brain areas.

That is the short version. These medicines change signals; they do not supply a personal explanation for every sensation. A smaller appetite does not prove that you are eating enough, that you are eating too little, or that a new symptom is harmless. It is one observation to discuss with your care team, not a verdict about your effort or your health.

The medicine’s approved purpose also matters. Some people are prescribed a product for weight management; others may have a type 2 diabetes-related indication or another product-specific approved use. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration does not give one shared list of indications to every medicine that happens to contain semaglutide or tirzepatide. For instance, the current labels include uses beyond weight management for some products, including cardiovascular-risk reduction or treatment of moderate-to-severe sleep apnea in particular groups. Wegovy’s current label also includes an indication related to certain adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a liver disease. The exact conditions and eligible groups are product-specific.

A brand pair is not a permission slip to borrow another product’s indications. An indication listed for Wegovy does not automatically apply to Ozempic; the same is true of Zepbound and Mounjaro. Your prescriber may have a reason for the product chosen, and this book cannot judge that reason. If you are not sure which purpose applies to your prescription, ask: “What condition is this product treating for me, and where can I read that in its current FDA label?”

Common does not mean imaginary

Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation and abdominal discomfort or pain appear among the common adverse reactions across these product labels. The exact common-effect list is not identical for every brand. Depending on the product, it may also include fatigue, indigestion, decreased appetite, reflux, burping or other effects. Check the current label for your own medicine rather than assuming a list copied from a different brand applies to you.

“Common” is a label category, not a dismissal. A symptom can be familiar and still interfere with eating, drinking, sleep or ordinary life. It can also have a cause that has nothing to do with the medicine. Don’t use a symptom list to diagnose yourself, and don’t wait out a severe or persistent problem because somebody online called it normal.

Reading the label without memorizing it

The full prescribing information is arranged in sections for a reason. “Indications and Usage” states the approved purpose and eligible group for that product. “Contraindications” names situations in which the label says the medicine should not be used. “Warnings and Precautions” describes important risks and what patients or clinicians should watch for. “Adverse Reactions” lists effects observed in the product’s clinical studies and other reported reactions. These are not interchangeable lists, and a short summary cannot carry every instruction in them.

The Medication Guide is the patient-facing companion to the full label. Start there if the prescribing information is dense. If a phrase or instruction is unclear, ask the pharmacist or prescriber to explain how it applies to you.

Labels also describe risks that depend on a person’s health history or other treatment. For example, low blood sugar is a particular concern when some of these medicines are used with insulin or certain other diabetes drugs; it is not a reason to assume that everyone taking one of these products will have a low. A history named under contraindications is not the same thing as a symptom to monitor. If you recognize a history that might apply, raise it with the prescriber or pharmacist promptly rather than trying to interpret a relative’s diagnosis or an old chart on your own.

The practical move is modest: note what you noticed, when it began, whether it is getting better or worse, and what question you want answered. The observation-versus-decision distinction from the introduction still matters here. A note helps a conversation; it does not authorize a change to food, other medicines or your prescription. If a symptom is troubling, keeps returning, or makes it hard to keep fluids down, contact your prescriber or pharmacist for advice tailored to you. If it feels urgent, use the emergency guidance in your current Medication Guide or seek urgent care. You do not need to prove that a symptom is serious before asking for help.

Match the brand on your box to its current Medication Guide. The two-tier card below helps you decide how urgently to seek help; your pharmacist or prescriber can clarify what applies to your health and other medicines.

A two-tier warning card

Use the first tier for a possible emergency. The second is for warning signs that need prompt contact with your care team.

Call 911 or get emergency care now

  • Trouble breathing; swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat; fainting; or other signs of a severe allergic reaction.
  • Any symptom your current Medication Guide identifies as an emergency, or a severe, rapidly worsening symptom that makes you fear for your immediate safety.

A serious allergic reaction can include more than a rash. If breathing or throat swelling is involved, do not wait for an office callback. Use emergency services.

Call your prescriber urgently

  • For severe abdominal pain that will not go away, with or without vomiting or pain reaching your back, follow your own product’s Medication Guide: stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away. If you cannot reach them or the pain is severe or worsening, seek urgent or emergency care.
  • Pain in the upper abdomen, fever, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or pale stools. These can be signs of a gallbladder problem named in product warnings. Do not try to sort out the cause yourself.
  • Repeated vomiting or diarrhea, inability to keep fluids down, much less urination than usual, or other signs that concern you about dehydration or kidney problems. The labels warn that fluid loss can lead to kidney injury. Contact your care team promptly; if you are fainting, confused, rapidly worsening or unable to get help safely, seek emergency care.
  • Shakiness, sweating, confusion, dizziness or other possible low-blood-sugar symptoms, particularly if you also use insulin or certain other diabetes medicines. Follow the low-glucose plan your diabetes team gave you. If symptoms are severe, you cannot safely treat them, or you lose consciousness, get emergency help.
  • A lump or swelling in the neck, persistent hoarseness, or trouble swallowing. The current semaglutide and tirzepatide labels carry a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents; whether the medicines cause these tumors in people is unknown. The labels say not to use these products with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), a type of thyroid cancer, or with multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2), an inherited condition. If either history applies to you, contact your prescriber or pharmacist promptly to discuss your specific prescription. Do not try to decide on your own what the history means.
  • New or worsening vision changes, especially if you have diabetes, or another symptom your product’s Medication Guide tells you to report promptly. Tell the clinician what changed and when. Use emergency care for sudden severe vision loss or another immediately dangerous symptom.

The second tier means contact your prescribing team without delay for advice about what to do next; the right timing and route depend on the symptom and your care plan. If you cannot reach them and the symptom is getting worse, seek urgent or emergency care. This card is a prompt to get help, not a rule that you must wait for a prescriber before acting.

These four product labels also warn about serious allergic reactions, pancreatitis, gallbladder problems, hypoglycemia in some situations, kidney injury associated with dehydration, and thyroid C-cell tumors. Blood-sugar and vision instructions matter especially for people with diabetes.

Take the right page to the right person

A boxed warning is the FDA’s prominent warning for a serious risk; it does not predict that a particular patient will develop that problem.

If your medicine is used for type 2 diabetes, include your diabetes care team in questions about blood sugar and other glucose-lowering medicines. If you take other prescriptions, mention them to the pharmacist or prescriber; a side effect, a low reading or a new symptom may depend on the whole medication picture. This is especially important when more than one clinician is involved. No one is expected to reconstruct that list from memory while feeling unwell. Bring the list or a photo of it.

When an appointment feels rushed, use a short record rather than a theory. For example, suppose nausea has returned after dinner for several evenings. A note might read: “Since Tuesday, nausea has started after dinner and lasted about two hours. I vomited once on Wednesday. On Thursday I kept water down; urination was [usual/less than usual]. I also take [medicine names] and started [anything new] on [date]. Should I be seen, and what would make this urgent for me?” This is a reporting example, not a way to decide the medicine caused the symptom.

Put the start date and time beside each symptom, and note whether it is improving, worsening or unchanged. Include what you could eat and drink, any vomiting or diarrhea, other medicines, and a relevant recent change. If your diabetes team already asked you to track glucose, include the reading and time; do not delay care to collect one. Have the brand name and strength from the package nearby, plus the Medication Guide if available. If you reach a covering clinician, say the exact product name; similar active ingredients do not make the product instructions identical.

A compact message can end with a direct request: “Please tell me whether I should be seen today, who to call after hours, and which change means I should seek emergency care.” Write down the name of the person who answered and the next step they gave you. A pharmacist can help locate the correct product guide or review a medicine question; the prescriber can decide whether an assessment is needed. Do not hold up urgent care to finish the note. If the warning card says emergency care, or you cannot keep fluids down, act rather than waiting for an office callback.

If you leave a message, include a callback number and a safe time to reach you. Keep the package nearby in case the office asks you to read the product name or strength. If the advice is unclear, repeat back the next step in your own words before ending the call.

If you are already dealing with severe pain, breathing trouble, fainting, or another emergency sign, skip the appointment-prep exercise and get help. A tidy note is useful; it is never a prerequisite for care.

Before you turn the page

Keep the card beside your medicine list; if a warning sign appears, use it now.

Before you close the book, keep these two steps with your medicine list:

  • Contact your prescriber urgently about severe or persistent abdominal pain, gallbladder warning signs, inability to keep fluids down, possible low blood sugar, a neck lump or persistent hoarseness, vision changes, or another symptom the guide says to report.
  • Ask your pharmacist or prescriber to clarify what is specific to your health history and other medicines.

Chapter 11: Protein First

The grocery store was bright enough to make every label look urgent. It was week three. By three in the afternoon, I had managed half a burrito, and I was standing beside the carts trying to remember why I had come for eggs.

Then I felt lightheaded.

I set the basket down and sat. I did not know what had caused it, and I did not turn the moment into proof that one food or one missed meal explained everything. I called Anita’s office and described what I noticed. That is the part worth borrowing: report a symptom instead of naming its cause. Dizziness or fainting is not a cue to solve the problem with a snack and move on; if it happens to you, use the low-glucose instructions from your diabetes team, if you have them, and contact a clinician promptly.

The grocery trip changed how I planned food. I stopped waiting for hunger to remind me to eat and started putting a few small chances for protein on the day. Not a prescription. A reminder that appetite is not a reliable appointment calendar.

Start with a question, not a number

Protein helps build and maintain muscle, among other jobs in the body. In its guide to healthy eating for adults with chronic kidney disease, NIDDK explains that protein needs can differ and may change over time. It advises people with kidney disease to work with a dietitian or health professional to find the right amount and sources. That is a useful caution for this whole conversation: a number that suits someone else may not suit you.

This book does not set a gram target. The sources gathered for it do not establish one protein number for every person using a GLP-1 medicine. A target can depend on your health, the rest of your eating, and any instructions from your care team. If you have kidney disease or another condition that affects food choices, the target and the kinds of foods you use deserve particular care. Ask your prescriber or a registered dietitian who knows your history to help set it. A dietitian can also turn a target into foods and portions you can manage; that is far more useful than a number on a sticky note with no plan behind it.

You can open the conversation plainly: “My appetite is smaller, and I want to talk about protein while I am losing weight. Is a protein target appropriate for me? If so, what amount and food sources fit my health and other instructions?” If you already have a target, bring it back for a check if your health, appetite, or treatment plan has changed. Do not increase it on your own because a social post or a package promises a bigger result.

There is another reason to keep the conversation individualized. Protein is one part of maintaining nourishment during weight loss; it does not replace the individualized strength and activity discussion in Chapter 12 or advice from your care team. The NIDDK’s prescription-medications guidance describes these medicines as working alongside healthy eating and physical activity, not in place of either. Chapter 12 takes up strength work. Here, the job is narrower: make it easier to notice and plan a few protein-containing foods without turning meals into a math exam.

Make the day easier to see

When appetite is quiet, a large plate can look like a dare. I do better thinking in small checkpoints: an opportunity in the morning, another around midday, one later in the afternoon, and one at supper if it fits my day. Three or four is a planning frame, not a quota. Your clinician’s instructions come first, and there is no prize for forcing food when doing so conflicts with advice you have been given.

A checkpoint is simply a moment when you ask, “What small protein food could fit here?” It might be part of breakfast, a small snack, or a few bites alongside something else. The question is not whether you can finish a restaurant-size portion. It’s whether you have made a reasonable opportunity before the day gets away from you.

Try attaching the first checkpoint to a thing that already happens. If you take morning medicines with a clinician-approved breakfast, that may be a useful place to consider a protein food. If mornings are a sprint, pick a later anchor: the first pause at work, the time you make tea, or when you put lunch in the fridge. The anchor is a reminder, not a new medical schedule. If a medicine instruction, test, or care plan affects when you eat, follow that instruction and ask your care team how to fit food around it.

I used to treat the end of the day like a service rush: if I had not eaten much, I tried to make supper do all the work. That usually made the plate feel even bigger. A few modest opportunities are less intimidating than asking one meal to repair the whole day. It also gives you something concrete to report at an appointment: “Breakfast was difficult; I could manage yogurt later,” is more useful than “I never eat enough,” which is both hard to measure and easy to turn into blame.

Choose foods you will actually keep around

Protein does not require a special powder or a heroic cooking session. Think of familiar foods you can store, portion, and eat in the circumstances you actually have. Eggs, yogurt or cottage cheese, beans, tofu, fish, and cooked chicken are examples. The right choices depend on your preferences, allergies, budget, cultural foods, and any medical limits. NIDDK’s kidney-nutrition guidance, for example, explains that some people with chronic kidney disease may need to adjust the amount or source of protein with a health professional. A general list is a starting shelf, not an instruction to eat every item on it.

Keep convenience honest. A ready-to-eat food can be useful even if it is not an impressive recipe. A single-serving cup, a container of beans, or leftovers already divided into a small portion can lower the number of steps between you and a bite. If a food needs more work than you can face, it is not a practical option for that moment. I am a cook by temperament; I still know that “just prepare something” is useless advice when the cutting board feels like a project.

A protein food can share the plate with whatever else is manageable. A few spoonfuls of yogurt beside fruit, an egg with toast, beans with rice, or some chicken tucked into soup are examples of combinations, not complete meal plans. If your clinician has asked you to follow a specific eating plan, use that plan rather than these illustrations. The goal is not to make every bite carry a nutritional assignment. The goal is to have a couple of low-friction options available when appetite gives you little notice.

Choose two or three options for the week instead of buying a new shelf of products. Think about what keeps, what you already like, and what takes almost no assembly. If you shop once a week, put one shelf-stable choice in the pantry and one ready-to-eat choice where you can see it. If food cost is tight, tell the dietitian or clinic plainly; the plan needs to fit your budget, not an imaginary one. Frozen, canned, and dried foods may be useful depending on your needs and the instructions you have been given.

Make portions smaller without making the plan smaller

A checkpoint does not need to be a full meal. Put a small portion on a plate or in a cup, then give yourself permission to stop when you are done. You can decide later whether another small portion makes sense. Nothing here asks you to push through discomfort or ignore a symptom. If eating is repeatedly difficult or you are worried about getting enough, bring that to your prescriber or dietitian; they can help you consider the full picture.

It can help to keep a short note for several ordinary days. Write the time and the food, and, if you already have an individualized target, note how the food fits it. Leave out calorie scoring and moral grades. You are looking for a pattern you can discuss: perhaps the morning checkpoint is consistently missing, or maybe one portable food works better than a cooked meal at lunch. One day is not a verdict. It is a sample.

If you prefer not to track, use a simple visual cue. Put a small mark beside each planned checkpoint on your calendar or phone. The mark means “I paused to consider a protein food,” not “I passed.” If the calendar stays blank, look at the setup: the reminder may be late, or the food may not have been ready. Change the setup, not the story you tell about your character.

The schedule should bend around real life. If you have a morning appointment, a long commute, or a shift with few breaks, plan the most dependable checkpoint first. Pack a food you know you can store safely, if that works for your situation. If food access or storage is a problem, say so when you speak with your care team. A plan that assumes a refrigerator you do not have will fail for a reason unrelated to effort.

When the usual food list does not fit

Some readers have food allergies, religious or cultural restrictions, limited budgets, swallowing or dental problems, kidney disease, diabetes meal instructions, or other conditions that change the choices. Do not squeeze yourself into a generic list. NIDDK notes that chronic kidney disease can change protein needs and that some people may need to limit or adjust protein, while others, including some people receiving dialysis, may need a different approach. That example is why a clinician or dietitian should help set a target when a medical condition affects nutrition.

If dairy does not suit you, it does not follow that you have failed the chapter. If meat is not part of your diet, plant foods can be discussed as sources with your dietitian. If a supplement seems easier than food, ask your clinician or pharmacist whether a particular product fits your health, medicines, and any restrictions; the label’s front is not a personal assessment. You do not need to buy anything to begin this conversation.

The same goes for a day when almost nothing sounds good. This chapter is not a treatment plan for nausea or other side effects, and a protein checklist is not a reason to wait out a symptom. Chapter 13 covers what to track and report when side effects interfere with eating. If you cannot keep fluids down, feel faint, or have a severe or worsening symptom, use the Chapter 10 warning card and contact your care team or emergency services as directed. Call a health professional when the pattern is interfering with eating or your health; do not try to solve it by forcing a new target.

Make a target usable outside the appointment

A target only helps if it fits the places where you eat. The appointment is a good place to say what those places look like, not just to ask for a number. Do you have a refrigerator at work? Can you take breaks when you need them? Is the kitchen shared? Does the grocery trip happen on foot, by bus, or as part of someone else’s errand? Those details are part of nutrition planning, not evidence that you lack discipline.

If you can meet with a registered dietitian, ask whether they can help translate an individualized protein discussion into choices that fit your health, budget, preferences, and storage. Some clinics offer different ways to meet; ask what is available rather than assuming an appointment format or referral is available. If you are not sure how to find the right professional, ask the prescriber’s office who handles nutrition referrals for people with your conditions.

It may help to arrive with a rough map of an ordinary day. Not a polished food diary: just note where food is available, where it is not, and what makes a choice hard. For example, a person who works a long shift might have ten minutes between customers, a shared refrigerator, and no reliable way to heat lunch. Another might shop once a week and have little freezer space. Those are different planning problems. Naming them lets the dietitian ask which options are realistic without asking you to make up a story about why a plan did not work.

Ask the dietitian to separate three questions that can otherwise collapse into one: whether a target is appropriate for you, which sources fit your health and eating pattern, and what to do when the usual option is unavailable. With kidney disease, NIDDK says protein amounts and sources should be discussed with a dietitian or health professional; needs can differ and change. If another clinician has given you a food restriction, bring the exact instruction so the professionals can account for it rather than having you reconcile it alone.

The wording can stay simple: “Here is what I can usually keep and eat. Which of these choices fit the target you recommend, and what is a practical backup when they are not available?” If cost is tight, say so before the conversation turns into a shopping list. Ask which lower-cost options fit your plan and whether a clinic social worker or another local resource can help with access. Availability varies; the point is to describe the obstacle early, not to promise that a particular service exists.

Different constraints call for different questions. If you do not have dependable refrigeration, ask how the professional wants you to think about shelf-stable choices and safe storage. If chewing, swallowing, allergies, or nausea limits what works, describe the problem and ask which professional should address it. This book cannot decide whether a texture or packaged food is appropriate for your condition. It can help you bring the real limitation into the room instead of leaving with a plan designed for somebody else’s kitchen.

If your family eats differently, you do not have to replace the household menu to have this discussion. Bring the foods you actually cook or buy and ask where a manageable protein choice could fit alongside them. A familiar bean dish, tofu, fish, eggs, dairy, or meat may be worth discussing depending on your needs and preferences; the list is not a recommendation to use any particular item. A dietitian can help consider the full combination and any relevant medical limits.

If the clinician offers a specific target, make sure you understand whether it is a daily amount, a range, or something else they have chosen for you; this book will not supply or reinterpret the number. Ask how they want you to use it on a day when appetite is low, whether they want you to track anything, and when the target should be revisited if your health or care plan changes. If an answer is unclear, ask them to explain it in foods and examples rather than converting it yourself into a stricter rule.

There is no need to prepare a perfect record before asking for help. Bring the map of your real week, one food-access barrier, and the question that has been hardest to answer. Leave with the name of the person who can help with the next part, or with a clear question to take back to your prescriber. Then choose only the option that fits the instructions you were given.

If the barrier is access, not appetite

Food access can change from one week to the next. A grocery trip may depend on a ride, a benefit balance, work hours, or whether the nearest shop carries the foods you know. If the options you discussed with a dietitian are not available, tell them which part failed: the price, the trip, storage, preparation, or the food itself. A useful plan needs a backup for the barrier you actually have.

For an appointment, you could bring a short two-column note: “What I can get or store” and “What gets in the way.” Keep it concrete. “I can shop every other Friday and have one freezer drawer” gives a different picture than “I need to eat better.” If writing a list feels like work, say the details out loud. The professional can ask follow-up questions; you do not need to show up with a solution.

Ask what local help is available, but treat each suggestion as a lead to verify. A clinic might know about a social worker, food pantry, community meal service, benefits counselor, or transportation resource. These programs differ in eligibility, location, schedule, and what they provide. The prescriber’s office may not know every current detail, so call the program directly before planning around it. If the first resource cannot help, ask whether they know the next appropriate contact.

If a food pantry or community meal is part of the week, the dietitian can help you think through what is available without asking you to reject food you can access. You might ask, “Given my care plan, how should I choose among the options I actually receive?” Bring package labels or a menu only if they are easy to get; there is no requirement to document every meal. The purpose is to adapt the discussion to reality, not to make limited choices feel like a personal shortcoming.

If you share shopping or cooking with another person, ask for one defined kind of help. “Could you tell me before you use the yogurt I set aside?” or “Would you add the canned beans from this list if they are in stock?” leaves the request clear. Avoid making them responsible for checking whether you met a target. That target, if one is appropriate, belongs in the conversation with your clinician or dietitian.

Some readers have no stable place to store food or prepare it. In that case, don’t rely on advice that assumes a full kitchen. Ask the dietitian or clinic whether they can discuss options for your actual storage and food-safety situation. Do not keep perishable food without safe refrigeration because a checklist says it is convenient. Chapter 18 covers general leftovers and storage; the question here is which accessible choices fit your personal nutrition guidance.

The plan can include a sentence for the next visit: “The options we discussed were not available this week because ___. Could we make a backup using ___, or connect me with someone who helps with food access?” That gives the professional a problem they can respond to. A program, benefit, or particular food may not be available, but naming the barrier gives the discussion a place to start.

If access remains uncertain, keep the immediate food question separate from the target question. Ask what to do under your existing care instructions while you are trying to reach the dietitian, and who to contact if you are unable to eat or drink adequately. This book cannot decide how long you can wait or set an intake threshold. A worsening symptom or inability to keep fluids down belongs with the care team, not with a grocery workaround.

The protein-on-a-schedule checklist

Before you shop or plan tomorrow, put the clinician-approved target in the first line if you have one. If you do not, leave it blank and make that the question for your prescriber or dietitian. Then pick three or four possible checkpoints and name one manageable food for each. These are options to consider, not obligations; follow your personal care instructions.

  • My protein target, if set with my care team: ______.
  • Morning or first dependable pause: ______.
  • Midday pause: ______.
  • Afternoon pause: ______.
  • Evening option, if it fits my instructions: ______.
  • One food I can keep ready without much work: ______.
  • One question I want to ask my prescriber or dietitian: ______.

On a hard day, reduce the size of the task. A spoonful, a few bites, or a small container you can return to later may be a more workable starting point than a full plate, if that fits your care plan. If the checklist starts to feel like a demand, set it down and tell your clinician what is getting in the way. You are collecting useful information, not grading your appetite.

I still think about that grocery-store basket, left beside the carts while I sat and made a call. The lesson was not that a particular food explains lightheadedness. I did not know the cause. The lesson was that a quiet appetite can make it easy to miss the ordinary chances to eat, so I now make those chances visible and ask for help when the body does something I cannot explain.

Before your next grocery trip, write down one protein food you can manage tomorrow and one question about your target. Put both on the list.

Chapter 12: Don’t Lose the Muscle

The flour sack had the same label it always did: fifty pounds, white paper, a blue stripe down the side. I got my hands under it at the bakery and lifted. The bag cleared the floor. The stairs were another matter. I couldn’t haul it up the way I used to, and I stood there longer than I needed to, pretending to check the prep list.

That moment bothered me more than a number on a scale. I wanted to know what my body could still do on an ordinary workday. Lou, who was already a regular at the rec center, invited me to come along. He didn’t hand me a workout plan or tell me what my body needed. He showed me where the strength room was, and we asked the staff how to get an orientation. I started with movements that felt manageable and learned to make the room less mysterious.

I can’t say why that sack felt different on that day. A book can’t diagnose a change in strength, and a single lift cannot tell you how much muscle you have. But noticing a change gave me a useful question for my clinician: what kind of strength work is appropriate for me now?

Strength belongs in the plan early

Weight can change faster than your routines do. Your appetite may be quieter, your clothes may fit differently, and the scale may offer a steady stream of numbers. None of those tells you whether carrying laundry, getting out of a low chair, climbing stairs, or opening a stubborn jar is getting easier or harder.

Strength work deserves a place while weight is changing, not just after you reach a number you had in mind. It is one way to practice using your muscles against resistance. A list of movements cannot tell you what will happen to your muscle during weight loss. It does give you a practical habit to discuss and build around your own body, abilities, and medical advice.

NIDDK says weight-management medicines do not take the place of physical activity or healthy eating, and work best within a lifestyle program. The federal physical activity guidelines, linked from NIDDK’s page for prescription weight-management medicines, set a broad reference point: adults should aim for at least two days a week of muscle-strengthening activity, along with at least 150 minutes a week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity. That’s a public-health guideline, not a personal clearance or a demand to start at full pace tomorrow. Your starting point may need to be different.

If you use a cane, have joint pain, neuropathy, heart or lung disease, a history of falls, or a long gap in activity, don’t treat a general guideline as a dare. Tell your prescriber what you hope to do and ask whether a physical therapist or another qualified professional should help you choose safe movements. A physical therapist can assess movement and balance, show you how to adjust an exercise, and help you work within a restriction. That is a better use of expertise than copying the strongest person in the room.

Pause for a readiness check

Before starting a new strength routine, use this clearance rule: if you have chest pain, dizziness, a recent injury or surgery, severe balance problems, uncontrolled blood sugar, or activity limits set by your clinician, ask your prescriber or a physical therapist what is safe for you. If you have several conditions or aren’t sure which clinician to ask, start with the person who knows your medical history and request a referral if needed.

Be specific when you ask. “Can I exercise?” is a broad question, and a rushed answer may not tell you what to do next. Try: “I’d like to do some basic strength work at home or at the rec center. I have [condition, symptom, injury, or restriction]. Are there movements I should avoid, and should I see a physical therapist first?” Mention recent falls, pain that changes how you move, and any directions you already received about activity. Bring a written list if names or dates are hard to recall in the appointment.

If you are already cleared for activity, but one movement feels uncertain, ask a physical therapist, exercise professional at the facility, or clinician to show you a safer variation. A sturdy chair and a wall can be useful tools; they do not make an exercise automatically safe. The floor, chair, band, and load all matter. So does your balance that day.

During activity, stop for chest pain, fainting, or another sudden, severe symptom and seek urgent care. If you develop dizziness, unusual shortness of breath, pain that changes your movement, or a symptom that worries you, stop the movement and contact a health professional for advice before trying to push through. If it feels like an emergency, use emergency services. Don’t wait to finish a workout, and don’t let embarrassment make the decision for you.

Four movements to discuss or adapt

These are examples, not a prescribed workout, and they are not suitable for every person. Choose only movements that fit your clearance and ability. A physical therapist or qualified professional can show you how to adjust them. You don’t need to do all four, and this book isn’t assigning repetitions, weight, or a progression schedule.

  • Sit-to-stand: From a stable chair, practice rising and sitting with control. Using your hands for support or choosing a higher seat may be an option to discuss if the movement is difficult. Keep the chair from sliding, and don’t use this example if standing challenges your balance.
  • Wall push-up: Face a clear wall and place your hands at a comfortable height. Moving closer to or farther from the wall changes how demanding the movement feels. If you have shoulder, wrist, or balance concerns, ask for a suitable alternative rather than testing it alone.
  • Band row: A resistance band can provide a pulling movement without a weight machine. The band and its anchor must be in good condition and secured according to its instructions; a band that slips or snaps can injure someone. If you don’t know how to set it up, have a professional demonstrate it first.
  • Farmer carry with a grocery bag: Carrying a light bag for a short, clear path resembles a task many people already do. The bag is an example of a household object, not a suggested weight. Skip it if carrying affects your balance, grip, pain, or walking; ask about a safer substitute.

The setup matters as much as the name of a movement. A chair on a rug can slide. A band anchored to a loose door handle can pull free. A bag that is easy to lift on one side may twist your body. Clear the space, use equipment as its maker instructs, and get another set of eyes on a movement if you’re uncertain. There is no prize for making a home exercise look like the version on a video.

If you’re working with a physical therapist, follow the plan they give you rather than this list. At a gym, staff can orient you to equipment and facility rules; they cannot clear a medical restriction or choose movements for a health condition. Ask your clinician or physical therapist to adapt a movement. An online demonstration cannot see the way you move or what hurts.

What a facility orientation can and cannot do

An orientation at a rec center or gym can make equipment less unfamiliar. It is not a medical assessment and it cannot clear an injury, explain a new symptom, or replace an activity limit from your clinician. If a health condition or restriction is part of the question, take that to the clinician or physical therapist first. Once you know what kind of activity fits, facility staff can explain how the room works, where equipment is, and which local rules apply.

Before you book, ask what the orientation includes and who will lead it. Some places offer a walk-through; others demonstrate equipment or explain how to adjust it. Do not assume the word “orientation” means an individual exercise plan. Tell the staff member what you are asking for: “I have a plan from my physical therapist and want to learn the equipment that matches it,” or “I’m new to this room and would like to know how to use the machines safely.” If you are not sure whether an instruction is medical or simply about the equipment, pause and check with the person who set the restriction.

Bring the written movement limits or the name of the professional who gave them, if you have that information. You do not need to disclose your entire history to the front desk. Share only what helps staff answer the practical question, and ask the clinician what they want you to tell a trainer or facility worker. If the proposed equipment or movement does not match the plan you were given, do not let politeness make you try it. Ask for an alternative that does fit, or leave that question for your clinician.

The room itself can be part of the decision. Is there a stable route from the entrance to the equipment? Can you pause without blocking other people? Is there seating nearby? Are instructions large enough to read? If hearing or vision makes demonstrations difficult, ask whether staff can explain the equipment another way. If you use a mobility aid, ask the facility about storage and accessible routes before you arrive. These are logistics, not signs that you need to prove anything before you belong there.

Cost and access count too. Ask whether the orientation is included, whether there is a fee, and whether you can see the room before joining. If the facility is not affordable or reachable, tell your clinician what is realistic. They may be able to suggest a physical therapist, a community program, or another resource, but availability differs by location and insurance. A suggestion is not a promise that a service is covered or open to you.

On the day, you can keep the visit narrow: learn the entrance, locate the equipment named in your plan, and find out whom to ask about a loose strap or an unclear setting. If the room is crowded or the staff member is rushed, reschedule the orientation instead of letting embarrassment turn it into an improvised workout. You can leave with the room still unfamiliar. That is safer than turning a walk-through into an unsupervised test of what your body can tolerate.

Give a function goal a real setting

“Get stronger” is a broad hope. A task gives your clinician or physical therapist something specific to discuss. Maybe you want to stand from the low chair at your kitchen table without grabbing the counter. Maybe the grocery tote has become awkward on the walk from the car. Maybe stairs are the hard part after a long work shift. Those are examples of priorities, not home assessments and not proof that a medicine has changed your muscle.

Describe the task in its ordinary setting. How often does it come up? What part feels difficult: starting the movement, balance, pain, grip, or getting tired? Did something change recently, or has this been a long-standing limitation? Don’t repeat a movement that feels unsafe just to gather better evidence. Your clinician can decide what details are useful and whether a physical therapist should assess it.

Different descriptions lead to different conversations. Someone who feels unsteady stepping off a curb may need to discuss balance and fall risk before choosing a strength activity. Someone whose hands hurt while opening jars may need help identifying whether the concern is grip, joint pain, or something else. Someone returning after surgery should follow the surgeon’s activity restrictions rather than using a general exercise list. The book cannot tell which explanation applies; it can help you say what task has changed and ask who should evaluate it.

Keep the goal modest enough to recognize without turning it into a challenge. You might note, “I used the rail on the stairs today,” or “I carried the small bag with both hands.” Those are observations. Do not add repetitions, weight, or distance as a self-designed test. If a task is getting harder or a new symptom is involved, tell the clinician rather than waiting for a planned workout review.

You can also choose a goal that is not about lifting anything. Getting to the bus stop, reaching a shelf, standing long enough to cook, or keeping balance while dressing may matter more than a gym machine. Explain why the task matters in your life. A physical therapist can use that context when discussing movement choices; a trainer’s demonstration may help with technique only after your health-related limits are understood.

The question can be direct: “I want to keep doing [task] at home. What should be assessed, and is there a kind of professional who can help me work toward it safely?” If your ability changes sharply, you fall, or symptoms make the task unsafe, contact your care team promptly. You do not need a workout log or a comparison with last month before raising the concern.

When you leave the conversation, write down the task you named and the professional who will address it. If the next step is a referral, ask whom to call and what to do if access is delayed. If the plan is to continue an activity you already do, repeat back the limits that matter to you. This is not the appointment paperwork from the plateau chapter; the question here is how to keep a specific daily task in view while you learn what movement fits.

The flour sack made me think about a work task, but your meaningful task may be quieter. Write it in the first line of your next exercise note. Under it, put one question for the person who can help you decide what to do with it.

Make the week repeatable

The federal guideline’s two muscle-strengthening days can sound like a large commitment if your calendar is already packed. Think of it as a direction for the week, not a test you pass by doing a punishing session. If you’ve been cleared, choose two days with room between them and put a modest appointment on the calendar. It can be brief. The point is to make strength work visible enough that it isn’t postponed until an imaginary calmer month.

If two days are not a safe or realistic starting point for you, ask your clinician what first step fits. The right answer may involve a physical therapist, a different movement, or waiting until a health issue is addressed. Do not turn a public guideline into a reason to ignore pain, medical restrictions, or a body that is telling you to stop.

On a day when you feel well, the plan can still be smaller than your ambition. A short session that fits your clearance may be easier to repeat than a long one you dread. When a day goes sideways, don’t make up for it with extra work the next day. Return to the plan your care professional approved, or ask them how to adjust it if your symptoms or circumstances have changed.

Strength work is not the same as aerobic activity. The NIDDK guidance describes both: muscle-strengthening activity at least two days weekly and at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity weekly for adults. Those are broad guidelines, not a bespoke prescription. Walking, for example, may count toward aerobic activity for some people, but walking does not automatically replace strength work. If you have limits, ask your clinician how the recommendations translate to your situation.

I put my two possible strength days beside appointments and work shifts. If the rec center was out of the way, I picked a cleared-at-home option instead. (I did not do this the first time.) I stopped treating the plan as a promise to become a different person. It was a small slot in the week, the same way I set aside time to shop before the refrigerator was empty.

When you are restarting after time away

A return after illness, surgery, a long work stretch, or a caregiving season is not the same as beginning from the old routine. The plan that fit before may no longer match your current ability. If a clinician gave you restrictions, ask them when and how they should be reviewed; don’t assume the restriction has expired because the calendar moved on. After surgery or a new diagnosis, the professional responsible for that care should guide the return.

If you have simply been away from activity and have no new symptoms or medical restrictions, you still do not need to recreate your old schedule on the first day. Start by asking what part of your former routine you can resume safely, especially if your health or medicines changed during the break. A clinician or physical therapist can help if you are uncertain. There is no universal ramp-up schedule in this book, and I won’t turn a public activity guideline into one.

It helps to identify why you stopped. Was the room too far away, did your shift change, did an injury interrupt the plan, or did the routine take more time than you had? Those require different repairs. A bus route may call for a home option already cleared for you; an injury may call for clinical advice; a schedule problem may be solved by choosing another time. Name the reason before picking the replacement.

If you used to attend a class or follow a video, do not assume it remains appropriate after a health change. Ask the instructor whether a movement can be modified only after you know what limits your clinician wants respected. An online class cannot see a new balance problem or know your surgical restrictions. If there is pain, dizziness, a fall, or another new symptom, pause and get advice rather than testing whether the old version still works.

Returning to a facility can be an access problem too. Ask whether your membership is active, whether orientation is available after an absence, and how to arrange equipment help. If cost has changed, ask the center whether it has a lower-cost option or community access hours, and verify the terms directly. The facility may not have a program; your clinician or local community center may know another route, but availability varies.

When you talk with a physical therapist, bring the daily task that prompted you to return and what has changed since the previous plan. Ask whether the old goal still makes sense, which limits remain, and what sign means you should stop and call. Write down their words rather than translating them into a heavier load or more repetitions. If you do not understand a movement, ask for a demonstration or a simpler explanation before practicing alone.

There is no shame in returning through a conversation instead of through a workout. My first trip with Lou was partly about finding the room and asking for an orientation. The practical win was knowing where to go next, not proving that I could lift the flour sack again. If you have been away, choose one next contact or one question about the task that matters to you, then let the professional help define what follows.

Measure function, not just effort

A workout log can be plain. Write the date, what you tried, whether it felt comfortable, and any symptom or pain that changed how you moved. If a clinician gave you boundaries, note those too. The log is for noticing patterns and making a useful conversation; it is not a scorecard and should not be used to increase a load or change a medical plan on your own.

Pay attention to ordinary tasks without turning them into home tests. Maybe standing from your usual chair takes less effort. Maybe carrying a small grocery bag still feels awkward. Those observations can help your clinician or therapist understand what matters to you. Don’t repeatedly test a difficult movement to prove a point, especially if pain, dizziness, or unsteadiness is involved.

If your strength seems to be dropping, you are falling, or daily tasks are becoming harder, contact your prescriber. Tell them what changed and when. They can consider whether you need an assessment, a referral, or another kind of support. A trainer can help with exercise technique within their scope, but a new or worsening health symptom belongs with a health professional.

Food and recovery matter to a whole health plan, but I won’t turn this chapter into another protein checklist. Chapter 11 covers how to discuss an individualized protein target. Bring any difficulty eating, unexplained weakness, or concern about what you can manage to your care team; strength work isn’t a substitute for that conversation. The useful approach is coordinated: ask one person who knows your health, make a plan that fits your body, and report changes instead of trying to troubleshoot a symptom alone.

A two-day strength-start checklist

Use this as a planning page, not a prescription. Fill it out after you have addressed the readiness check and any limits from your clinician.

  • The clinician or professional I will ask, if I need clearance: ______.
  • My current movement limits or symptoms to mention: ______.
  • Two possible days for cleared strength activity: ______ and ______.
  • One movement I can ask a professional to demonstrate or adapt: ______.
  • The stop signs I will respect: chest pain, losing consciousness, or another sudden, severe change.
  • One ordinary task I want to feel more capable doing: ______.
  • The date I will review this plan with my care team, if needed: ______.

You are not behind if your plan starts with a call, a referral, or learning how to get safely out of a chair. You are not failing if the federal guideline is not your current starting point. Keep the part you can act on: before your next workout, write down one movement you want a professional to check and ask for that help.

Sources

  • NIDDK, guidance on prescription treatment for overweight and obesity, including the linked federal physical activity guidance.

Chapter 13: Eating Around Side Effects

The Thanksgiving plates were still warm when I went back for seconds. I had recently had a dose change, and I ate quickly because everyone else was already halfway through dinner. That night, I was sick for hours.

The next morning I told Anita what happened. I couldn’t tell her whether it was the amount, the speed, the medicine change, the meal, or something else. I had a sequence of events, not a diagnosis. That distinction mattered. I needed her help interpreting the night, not a confident guess from me about what to cut out or change.

Side effects can make eating feel like a puzzle with missing pieces. This chapter is about keeping a useful record and reporting what you notice. It isn’t a list of foods that treat nausea, constipation, or heartburn. I don’t have verified evidence for a food remedy to recommend, and a remedy that suits one person may not fit another person’s health or care instructions.

Common is a label, not a verdict

Nausea, constipation, vomiting and abdominal discomfort appear among common adverse reactions in the current labels for several semaglutide and tirzepatide products. The wording and the full list vary by brand. The current Zepbound label, for example, includes gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) among common adverse reactions; the Mounjaro label uses indigestion in its list. Those terms are not a diagnosis for your particular burning or discomfort. Use the name you would use when telling your clinician what you feel, and check the Medication Guide for the exact product you take.

The word “common” doesn’t tell you how serious a symptom is for you, whether it has another cause, or what you should do about it. A symptom that appears in a label can still make it hard to eat, sleep, work, or care for yourself. And a bad night after a meal or dose change doesn’t prove which event caused it. Keep those questions open until you can discuss them with someone who knows your treatment and health history.

Chapter 10 has the two-tier warning card for signs that call for urgent or emergency attention. Use it rather than trying to solve a warning sign with a food experiment. If symptoms are severe, persistent, getting worse, or interfering with eating or drinking, contact your prescriber for guidance. Follow any specific instructions your care team has already given you, including instructions about whom to contact and when. If you cannot reach the office and the situation feels urgent, use the care route in your Medication Guide or seek urgent help. Don’t wait to finish a food log first.

Keep an observation, not a theory

A few plain details can make a short appointment message much more useful. Record what happened before you decide what it means. You don’t need to calculate calories or weigh a plate. A rough description is enough: a small bowl of soup, most of a sandwich, a few bites of a holiday meal. If you don’t remember an amount, write that down instead of inventing precision.

For a few days when symptoms are happening, note the time you ate, what you ate, roughly how much, and how long the meal took. Note when the symptom began, what it felt like in your own words, how long it lasted, and whether it eased, stayed the same, or worsened. If vomiting or a bowel change occurred, include that fact. You can also note whether you were able to keep fluids down, without turning this into a fluid target; Chapter 14 handles the separate hydration plan.

Add treatment context that may help your care team: when a dose change was made according to your prescriber’s instructions, any other recent medicine change, and whether anything else unusual was going on. Don’t record or change your dose as an experiment. Don’t delay care to fill in missing details, and don’t try to reproduce a meal or symptom to see if you can confirm a pattern.

The point isn’t to build a case against a particular food. It’s to give the clinician a clearer picture than “my stomach is bad.” If several episodes happen after different meals, that is useful too. If the symptom arrived without an obvious food connection, that is useful. An honest blank is better information than a tidy story you had to make up.

You don’t need to turn every meal into a report. Start with the episodes that matter to you, and follow any tracking instructions your care team has already given. If you already keep a blood-sugar log or another symptom record, ask whether they want this added there or kept separate. More detail is not automatically better if taking it makes you anxious or delays a call. The record should make a conversation easier, not become another job you can fail.

Context can help without becoming a theory. If you were sick, unusually tired, traveling, or taking another medicine differently, note that if you know it. If you don’t know whether it matters, let the clinician decide. A short note like “ate at 6:30; burning began around 8; meal was different from usual; no vomiting” can be more useful than a page of guesses about ingredients. Don’t make yourself inspect labels or reconstruct a recipe while you feel unwell.

If you are writing on a phone, use whatever privacy settings you normally use for health information. If someone helps you remember details, ask them to write only what you want shared. The goal is a record you can comfortably bring to an appointment or read over the phone, not a public food diary.

Notice the meal without blaming it

When appetite is small, it’s tempting to blame the last thing you ate. Sometimes the timing looks convincing: a symptom starts after dinner, so dinner must be the reason. But timing alone doesn’t identify a cause. A medicine effect, another medicine, an illness, a meal, or more than one factor could be involved. The log is a way to bring observations to your prescriber, not a home test that can sort those possibilities out.

For the same reason, don’t make a long list of foods forbidden based on one difficult evening. A list that grows after every symptom can leave you with fewer choices without answering the medical question. Don’t force yourself to eat through discomfort, either. Write down what you could manage and what happened, then ask your care team what they want you to do. If your prescriber or dietitian has already given you an eating plan, follow that individualized guidance rather than a general example here.

If a symptom keeps returning around meals, describe the pattern without presenting it as proof. You might say, “I’ve had a burning feeling after dinner on three evenings. It began about an hour later and lasted until bedtime. The meals were different. What should I do, and does this need an appointment?” The wording keeps what you observed separate from what you suspect. Your clinician can ask follow-up questions and decide whether you need an assessment.

Constipation can feel especially difficult to discuss because people often arrive having already tried several things. You can describe the change in your own words, when it began, what else changed, and how it is affecting you. If you have a care plan for this symptom, follow it; if you don’t, ask before adding a remedy or supplement. This chapter won’t prescribe a food, drink, over-the-counter product, or supplement as a fix. Your other conditions and medicines matter, and a pharmacist or prescriber can help you check a specific product.

The same restraint applies to nausea and reflux-like symptoms. I know the internet loves a universal fix. Your prescriber’s instructions and the product’s current Medication Guide are better starting points than a confident stranger’s menu. If you are unsure whether a symptom is covered by your instructions, send a message or call and ask. The question can be short. You are not required to arrive with a solution.

Report a rough night after a change

At Thanksgiving, I woke up with the details still out of order: the meal had gone fast, the plate was generous, and I had recently had a dose change. I told Anita the next morning. I didn’t say the change caused the night or promise myself I’d never eat those foods again. I told her what I remembered and asked what she wanted me to watch for.

That report gave us something concrete to discuss. It did not turn my story into evidence that the same meal or experience will affect you the same way. If you have a rough night after a dose change, report the timing and symptoms to your prescriber, especially if they persist or interfere with eating or drinking. Follow the instructions your prescriber gave you for the change. This book cannot tell you whether to delay, repeat, raise, lower, or stop a dose; those decisions belong with the person managing your care.

An appointment message can be simple:

“I followed the dose-change instructions we discussed on [date]. On [date/time], I ate [rough description]. Around [time], I noticed [symptom in my own words]. It lasted [duration] and is now [better/same/worse]. I [did/did not] vomit, and I [could/could not] keep fluids down. I also take [other medicines] and had [other recent change, if any]. What should I do next, and when should I seek urgent care?”

You can leave out details you don’t know. Keep a photo of the product name or the Medication Guide nearby if you need it, and include a callback number. If the office replies with instructions, write down who answered and the next step. If the message exchange leaves you uncertain, ask them to say plainly what would mean you need same-day attention or emergency care. The warning card in Chapter 10 remains the reference for urgent signs; don’t use a routine portal message for an emergency.

If you are unsure whether to wait for a routine appointment, say so directly: “This is interfering with eating and drinking. Do I need same-day advice or an assessment?” You are asking the care team to set the urgency for your situation, not deciding it from a checklist in a book. If symptoms are severe or worsening, don’t wait for a routine portal reply; use the contact instructions you were given, call the office, or seek urgent care as appropriate. For emergency warning signs, use emergency services.

If the answer involves a change to your medicine, make sure you understand the instruction and who is responsible for follow-up. Read it back in your own words: “So I should [repeat their instruction], and contact you again if [the condition they named]. Is that right?” Keep the instruction with your medication information. This is not a way to negotiate a different dose; it is a check that you understood the clinician’s plan. If the instruction conflicts with something on your product guide or with advice from another clinician, pause and clarify before acting, unless the guide says to seek emergency care now.

A food-and-symptom note for the next appointment

Use this as a record, not a food rule. It can be on paper or in a phone note. A few entries may be enough to describe what is happening; if care is needed sooner, contact the office rather than waiting to collect more.

  • Date and time I ate: ______.
  • Food and rough amount, or “not sure”: ______.
  • About how long I took to eat: ______.
  • Symptom, in my words, and when it began: ______.
  • How long it lasted; better, unchanged, or worse: ______.
  • Vomiting, bowel change, or difficulty keeping fluids down, if any: ______.
  • Dose-change date per my prescriber’s instructions, if relevant: ______.
  • Other recent medicine or health change to mention: ______.
  • My question for the prescriber: ______.

One note is not a pattern, and a pattern is not a diagnosis. Bring what you have. If the pages are mostly blank because the symptoms have been too disruptive to record, say that directly. It may be the most important detail.

Before the next dose-change conversation, put the symptom note where you can find it and write down one question for your prescriber. That is enough preparation for now.

Sources

  • Current product labeling and Medication Guides: Wegovy on DailyMed, Ozempic on DailyMed, Mounjaro on DailyMed, and Zepbound on DailyMed.

Chapter 14: Water and Electrolytes

The trail was dry and bright, and Teo kept asking if I wanted to stop. I said no. I hadn’t noticed how little I had drunk until the headache settled in. The next few days brought constipation, too, though I can’t prove the hike or the fluids caused it. I had a useful observation, not a diagnosis: I had gone a long stretch without drinking and hadn’t noticed.

After that, I stopped treating thirst as the only reminder I needed. Not because I know thirst disappears on a GLP-1 medicine. I don’t. Appetite and thirst are not the same signal, and I haven’t found evidence that these medicines reliably switch off thirst for everyone. But a quieter appetite, nausea, a busy day, or simply not having a drink nearby can make it easy to miss ordinary chances to drink. A routine can help without pretending to know what your body needs in ounces.

Build reminders, not a quota

There is no single daily fluid number in this book. Needs vary, and some people have been told to limit fluids because of a heart, kidney, or other health condition. If a clinician has given you a fluid limit or plan, use that rather than the reminders here. If you are not sure whether a limit applies, ask your prescriber or pharmacist before making a new target for yourself.

For everyone else, try attaching a drink to something already on the day: when you make breakfast, when you sit down for lunch, or when you take the afternoon break you already keep. Keep a cup or bottle where you can see it. Refill it when you clear a plate, if that fits your routine. These are prompts to notice drinking, not instructions to finish a particular container or force fluids when you feel unwell.

If a cue lands at a time when drinking feels uncomfortable, don’t turn it into a dare. Make a note of the symptom and ask your clinician what fits your situation, especially if it keeps happening or is limiting what you can drink. Chapter 13 explains how to record a symptom without guessing at its cause. This chapter’s routine is for ordinary days; it isn’t a treatment for nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

Use the drink you normally tolerate and that fits any guidance from your care team. This chapter does not prescribe a particular beverage, amount, electrolyte powder, sports drink, or supplement. If a product has an ingredient or mineral you need to limit, a pharmacist can help you check the label against your medicines and health conditions. A product marketed for hydration is not automatically appropriate for you.

One schedule and one product question

On an early shift, I keep a bottle beside my lunch bag; if the break disappears, my cue is clocking out. A new powder stays unopened until my pharmacist checks its label against my fluid and potassium limits. I ask: “Does this exact product fit the fluid and potassium limits you have on file for me?”

Put the written plan beside the cup

NIDDK’s CKD guidance, reviewed in January 2025 and checked in October 2026, says some people with kidney disease need an individual liquid limit; it also advises contacting a health professional about swelling. If your existing instructions are outdated, unclear or conflict with another clinician’s orders, ask the office that set the plan to resolve them in writing. Keep the confirmed wording and date with your medication list.

Then attach that instruction to the ordinary cue. For someone with a limit, breakfast can be the time to check the plan before pouring. The note uses the clinician’s terms rather than a bottle count invented here. My written plan says to check with the clinic if illness changes what I can drink; I put that phone number beside the breakfast cup.

A missed reminder doesn’t create a debt to repay by forcing a large drink. Leave the chart out of it. Keep the cup where you work and use the cue that asks the least of you.

Read the panel, not the promise

Turn a packaged drink around. The front may tell you what kind of day the maker thinks you want: athletic, busy, outdoors. The panel on the back tells you what is in the labeled serving. Those are different pieces of information. Here, reading the panel is a way to understand the package, not a way to choose a treatment for dehydration.

The FDA’s Nutrition Facts label-reading guide, dated March 2024 and checked in October 2026, says to start with serving size and servings per container. Nutrient amounts refer to that serving. The agency also makes a distinction worth remembering beside a water bottle: serving size describes an amount people typically consume; it is not a recommendation for how much you should drink.

That matters when the container and the serving are not the same. In a hypothetical bottle holding two labeled servings, the whole bottle contains twice the sodium and other nutrients listed for one serving. That is package arithmetic, not a daily fluid goal or a suggested serving. Before comparing two drinks, check what each panel is counting. Comparing one product’s bottle with another product’s smaller serving can make their contents look more alike than they are.

Some packages have separate columns for a serving and the entire container. The FDA describes these dual-column labels in the same guide. Read the heading above the numbers before copying them. “Per container” answers a different question from “per serving.” The bottle’s shape won’t settle it, and a container that fits neatly in your hand needn’t match the serving described on its panel.

Keep the units attached to any amount you copy. Sodium and potassium may be shown in milligrams; a beverage’s volume may be shown in fluid ounces or milliliters. Those describe different things. A number without its nutrient name or unit loses the information you were trying to preserve. If you take a photo, include the serving information above the nutrient lines rather than cropping down to one number.

The percentage beside a nutrient is its percent Daily Value. According to the FDA, it shows how much a serving contributes to a reference daily amount. It is not a percentage of your own kidney-care plan. NIDDK’s CKD guidance calls for individualized potassium and sodium advice. A general-reference percentage cannot tell you how much of a personal allowance remains, or whether a particular drink fits it.

Don’t let one front-label claim stand in for the whole panel. “No added sugar” doesn’t give you the sodium amount. A potassium amount doesn’t describe the drink’s total volume. Read the relevant lines separately. This is especially useful when two versions share a brand name but differ in flavor, formulation or package size: look at the container actually in your hand, not a saved picture of a similar one.

A powder introduces another distinction. The dry packet or scoop and the prepared drink are not interchangeable descriptions. Look for the labeled serving and the preparation directions, and keep both available for the product question above. Don’t infer that a larger mixing bottle changes how much mineral was in the packet. This book gives no homemade dilution recipe, and preparation directions are not instructions to treat illness.

You don’t need to transcribe the entire package. A readable picture of the panel, ingredient list and preparation directions preserves more than a note saying “hydration powder.” If part of the printing is hidden by a fold, smooth it out before photographing it.
